title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
description: Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.Pubs and shops in England
body: Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it. Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.The government wants digital ID apps under its scheme to work together so customers do not need to use different apps in different venues.It also wants the services to work offline and accessible even without mobile data or a Wi-Fi connection. In future, the digital proof of age scheme could be extended to cover tobacco and vapes.But digital rights campaigners have said such measures could lead to the exclusion of some groups.Jasleen Chaggar of Big Brother Watch said while having multiple ways to prove your identity was helpful, the Government should ensure that digital ID did not become effectively mandatory "as it would shut out millions of people"."Many people have legitimate reasons for relying on physical ID, whether out of choice, privacy and security concerns, or because they lack the digital skills or means to use digital ID," she said."The Government should expressly prohibit businesses from requiring digital IDs for age checks without offering reasonable alternatives," she added.The new rules come after a wider digital ID programme promoted by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer proved controversial, and was later abandoned by Andy Burnham.

schema.headline: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age

title: US confirms for first time it has deployed space weapons
description: The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities. US Secretary of the
body: The US has confirmed it deployed a space weapon in Earth's orbit, the first time it has acknowledged such offensive capabilities. US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action.Speaking at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference on Monday, Meink said the US was ready for "evolving threats", but did not elaborate on the weapon's capabilities or when it was put into orbit.Senior military leaders have previously said they planned to boost military capabilities in space, citing Russian and Chinese programmes developing ways to attack and disrupt US satellites in a future conflict. China responded on Tuesday by warning against an "arms race" in space. "We urge the US side to stop expanding its military capabilities and preparing for war in outer space," AFP quoted a foreign ministry spokesman as saying.Details of how the weapon operates have not been disclosed by US officials.A US Space Force spokesperson said: "Space control encapsulates the mission areas required to contest and control the space domain – employing kinetic and non-kinetic means to affect adversary capabilities through disruption, degradation and even destruction, if necessary. "These capabilities can be employed for offensive and defensive purposes at the direction of combatant commands."An expert on military uses of outer space noted that "precious little" was publicly known about the technology, and told the BBC there could be a "whole range of different weapons systems".Speaking to Radio 4's Today programme, Dr Bleddyn Bowen, from the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), said he was "totally guessing" but that the US could have been referring to "some kind electronic warfare or radio jamming platform". That would be the sort of weapon that already exists on Earth and could disrupt radio communications, Bowen said.An alternative would be "a kinetic kill vehicle of some sort - so a vehicle that would release a projectile of some sort that would ram into a satellite and destroy it". But this was less likely because such a physically destructive tool would be capable of creating a lot of debris, Bowen added.The Trump administration has said that space-based capabilities - and interceptor missiles - are a crucial part of its planned "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US from missiles and other airborne threats.Last year President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the US Space Force's role in not only defending assets, but also as an attacking force.The US Space Force - the first new branch of the US military for more than 70 years - was launched in 2019 as a way to protect American assets in space, including hundreds of satellites used for communication and surveillance. A 1967 treaty banned weapons of mass destruction in orbit. Since then, key powers including the US, Russia, and China have been exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation. In early February, it was revealed that two Russian satellites had likely intercepted the communications of at least a dozen European ones since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Such interceptions may have allowed Russian intelligence services to read the sensitive data they transmit, or hypothetically, even to take control of the satellites.In 2024, the US said Russia had launched a satellite which it believed may be capable of attacking other such probes. Russia did not publicly comment on the issue.The US Space Force says China "develops and operates space and counterspace capabilities as part of a military modernisation strategy," while Russia "views space as a warfighting domain and believes space supremacy will be a decisive factor in future conflicts".

schema.headline: US confirms for first time it has deployed space weapons

title: Nato jets shoot down drone that flew into Lithuanian airspace
description: Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.Authorities said the drone likel
body: Nato fighter pilots have shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace overnight, the Lithuanian president said.Authorities said the drone likely entered southern Lithuania, near the second-largest city of Kaunas, from neighbouring Belarus shortly after midnight on Tuesday.Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda wrote in a statement on X: "A drone that just entered Lithuanian airspace was destroyed by NATO fighter jets."The origins of the drone are yet to be determined, a spokesperson for the Lithuanian national crisis management centre said.Drone alerts sounded across the capital Vilnius and surrounding region earlier on Tuesday.Shortly after midnight local time (21:00 GMT), alerts were sent to phones in the region, warning of a potential drone incursion and telling residents to "find a safe place" and "wait for the all clear". Lithuania's armed forces and Italian pilots serving in the Nato Air Defence Mission "showed a swift and responsible response" to the drone incursion, Lithuania's Ministry of Defence said.Nausėda's post on social media added: "With Russia intensifying its aggression against Ukraine, such readiness is vital for our region. Together with our NATO Allies, Lithuania will defend its airspace."Moscow has not commented on the incident.Lithuania shares a large part of its southern and eastern border with Belarus, a key Russian ally.Drone sightings were reported in Lithuania on Sunday. The crisis management centre later said an object had "likely" entered from Belarus and travelled across the country's territory before entering the airspace of Russia. The 13 September incident did not trigger air threat alerts.Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine.Poland also announced there had been "aviation operations" in its airspace on Monday night "due to the activity of Russian Federation's jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicles conducting strikes on Ukrainian territory".These actions are of a "preventive nature" and are aimed at "securing airspace and its protection, especially in areas adjacent to threatened regions", it added.Residents in Lithuania's capital were forced to take shelter across Vilnius in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel.Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year.Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones.Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one NATO member shall be considered an attack against all members".

schema.headline: Nato jets shoot down drone that flew into Lithuanian airspace

title: Man admits drugging and raping wife over 20-year period
description: A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge over a 20-year period has admitted 60 offences against her.The husband, who cannot
body: A man accused of drugging and raping his wife without her knowledge over a 20-year period has admitted 60 offences against her.The husband, who cannot be named to protect his wife's legal right to anonymity, had already admitted some counts at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, including rape.The wife watched proceedings from the public gallery supported by members of her family.The husband, in his sixties, became visibly emotional as he repeated the word guilty to dozens of charges - including multiple counts of rape, assault by penetration and administering a substance with intent - and at one point was invited to sit down in the dock by the judge.Twelve other men deny multiple serious sexual offences against the same woman.The husband, from the Stockport area of Greater Manchester, will be sentenced for the counts he has admitted at the conclusion of the trial.A 13th man previously admitted sexual offences against the woman.The husband's offending against his wife, who he was married to for decades, took place over a period going back to 2004, while the accusations involving the other men range from September 2018 to November 2025.The other defendants are:Philip Wild, 58, from StockportSean Peers, 38, from StockportJordan Wallace, 31, from ManchesterAlan Keelan, 42, from ManchesterJonathan Kirk, 43, from StockportRobert Stewart, 70, from StockportMohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abodeGraham Brougham, 74, from Northwich, CheshireRichard Townsend, 37, from RochdaleKarl Lindsay, 55, Taunton, SomersetDaniel Rayner, 42, from, Whitstable, KentDavid Graves, 59, from, Ilkeston, DerbyshireThe trial is due to continue in the coming weeks.

schema.headline: Man admits drugging and raping wife over 20-year period

title: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school
description: Figure caption, ByRoyal correspondentThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security, following their
body: Figure caption, ByRoyal correspondentThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex are going to be given a review of their publicly-funded security, following their return to live in the UK.It is understood that the committee which oversees royal and VIP security, known as Ravec, is to reconsider Prince Harry and Meghan's level of police protection now that they and their two children are full-time residents rather than visitors.It will assess any risks they face in their new home and the type of trips taken by the couple and their family, such as regular travel routes and school runs.It has also emerged that the Sussexes have changed their children's school, only days after they first started, over security concerns about the school run.The schools' names have not been disclosed, but it is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had been concerned that the distance and the heavy traffic on the original school run route had made it difficult to make secure.A source close to the couple said: "The parents remain extremely grateful to all the teachers and staff for the love, care and effort they have shown their family. "This decision should in no way be interpreted as a reflection on the school or the exceptional care the children have received there."The prince previously mounted an unsuccessful legal challenge over his police security when he was visiting from the US.But the family's return to the UK has meant a different set of circumstances for their taxpayer-funded security, and last week the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - met to discuss their case.This committee, which includes representatives of the Home Office, the police and the Royal Household, seems ready to review potential dangers.This means a so-called Risk Management Board will consider the threats against them and the level of police protection they might need - although no final decision on the outcome has been reached.The review will include security for their children Archie, aged seven, and Lilibet, aged five, who started school earlier this month but, as first reported by HELLO! magazine, the children have switched schools because of a security issue.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Prince Harry and Meghan returned to the UK in late AugustIt is understood that Prince Harry had a review of his potential risks earlier in the summer, but before it was known that he would be returning to live in the UK.This will be the first such security review for Meghan since she and Prince Harry ceased being working royals when they moved to the US in 2020.Meghan posted footage on social media of the family at the weekend, showing a family outing in the countryside.Separately on Monday, Prince Harry was told that Uganda would now take part in the Invictus Games next year.It had appeared that Uganda was going to withdraw from the games for injured servicemen and women, in the fallout from a letter sent on behalf of King Charles emphasising that Prince Harry and Meghan remained non-working royals.The King's private secretary had spoken on the phone to Uganda's military chief, reassuring him that he approved of Uganda's participation in the games.

schema.headline: Harry and Meghan to have security review and children change school

title: Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'
description: Donald Trump Jr's wife, Bettina Trump, confirmed that their May wedding was paid for in part by an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.A post on
body: Donald Trump Jr's wife, Bettina Trump, confirmed that their May wedding was paid for in part by an ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.A post on her Instagram account – attributed to the couple – said that two nights of their three-day wedding festivities on a private island in the Bahamas were partially funded by Umar Kremlev, a Russian oligarch with close ties to Putin.The statement was released Monday after investigative journalism outlet ProPublica published a story detailing that Kremlev paid "hundreds of thousands of dollars" for the celebration.Donald Trump Jr, the president's eldest son, is a private citizen, so it is not illegal for him to accept gifts from a foreign national."Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding. It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful," the couple said in the statement.But ethics watchdog groups said it still presented the appearance of a conflict of interest for the president's son to accept lavish gifts from someone associated with a foreign head of state – even if he is not a US government employee."People don't just give hundreds of thousands of dollars to a random acquaintance without wanting something," said Jordan Libowitz, vice president of communications for Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (CREW)."You can see how [Putin] would enjoy all this press about how people in his circle are cozying up to people in the president's circle."According to the ProPublica article, the couple was married on a private island in the Bahamas, then held a two-day celebration on a separate island that rents for approximately $100,000 per night. Kremlev also paid other costs for the party, including a roughly $70,000 fireworks display, the report found.Kremlev runs the International Boxing Association (IBA), an organisation funded by the state-backed Gazprom energy company. The Olympic Committee suspended the group in part over its failure to report its ties to the Russian energy giant.Earlier this year Kremlev was part of a delegation that visited China with Putin. The Russian president also gave Kremlev the Order of Friendship, a top state honour, according to ProPublica.A spokesperson for Trump Jr told the news outlet that the president's son and Kremlev were personal friends and did not have "a business relationship".An ally of Trump Jr referred the BBC to the Instagram statement.In a statement to ProPublica, Kremlev's office said "Mr. Kremlev and Mr. Trump Jr have a friendly relationship." The statement said the men met a few years ago.Kremlev attended part of the wedding, the outlet reported. Other attendees included one of the US president's daughters, Ivanka Trump, and her husband, Jared Kushner, who has worked for the US on diplomatic negotiations with Iran, Russia and in the Middle East.The Trump campaign and family faced controversy for potential ties to Russia during the 2016 presidential election, resulting in a special counsel investigation. During the campaign Donald Trump Jr brokered a meeting at Trump Tower with a Russian operative that was closely scrutinised during the probe.Libowitz, of CREW, said either the president, who is a billionaire, or Trump Jr – who is worth $300 million, according to Forbes – could have paid for the full wedding to avoid a conflict of interest."His father is worth billions he could have picked up the tab. Clearly they just didn't want to pay for it," Libowitz said. "They don't really care about the ethical ramifications."

schema.headline: Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump say Putin ally paid for some wedding festivities as a 'gift'

title: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'free Palestine' speech
description: Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month. The artist - whose rea
body: Rapper Macklemore has been dropped from Ed Sheeran's US tour after making pro-Palestinian comments on stage earlier this month. The artist - whose real name is Benjamin Haggerty - had been the opening act for Sheeran's Loop tour, but was criticised by Jewish groups after saying "Free Palestine" at two concerts and making political speeches.Macklemore stood by his comments on Monday, confirming that he had been cut from the tour and writing in a statement that the real victims are the Palestinian people in Gaza.Ed Sheeran has not yet commented, and who will replace Macklemore for the rest of the tour is unknown.The controversy began on 4 September, when Macklemore, a long-time pro-Palestine activist, performed at Ed Sheeran's concert at the MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.He told the audience: "A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so that I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very, very dear to my heart: Free Palestine."He then performed his song Hind's Hall, which condemns Israel's military action in Gaza, while video footage of the devastation in Gaza was shown on the big screen.After that performance, the campaign group StopAntisemitism criticised the rapper, saying "Jewish fans bought tickets to see Ed Sheeran sing... not to be ambushed by Macklemore's anti-Israel propaganda."The next night, Macklemore returned to the same stage and directly addressed his "Jewish brothers and sisters" in the audience. "Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide, is in no way a criticism of you," he said, adding that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know they had not been forgotten.Israel rejects allegations of genocide. It says its troops conduct self-defence operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank in accordance with international law.The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to an unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage.During Israel's military campaign in Gaza more than 73,780 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.But the backlash against Macklemore only grew louder, and included a petition by the Israeli-American Council urging Sheeran to remove him from the tour. "This was an Ed Sheeran concert - not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event," the council said, adding that the rapper used "biased messaging and disputed claims."In his statement on Instagram, which was nearly 1,000 words long, Macklemore said that after a week of "difficult conversations" with Sheeran, that ultimately ended "in a place of fundamental disagreement", he was dropped from the lineup.Tour promoter, Messina Touring Group, told Rolling Stone magazine that it had been told by venues that they would not allow Macklemore to perform, "which would result in the cancellation of the tour and impact hundreds of thousands of fans."American businessman Robert Kraft, who owns the Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts, said he banned Macklemore because the venue would not "provide a platform for hate speech," accusing the rapper of "a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric"."I agree with Macklemore, too many lives have been lost and there has been too much suffering, but only sharing selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas is not honest and only advances more divisiveness and hate," Kraft said.In his statement, Macklemore said he empathised with the difficult position Sheeran was in, but criticised the English singer for not taking a stance."Taking a side can cost you. Money, brand deals, sponsorships, festivals, private shows, relationships and access. I've lost all of those things. But there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed," he wrote.He also addressed the accusations of antisemitism, writing that "one of the most effective ways to enforce silence has been to weaponize the accusation of antisemitism".Macklemore added: "When criticizing Israel, opposing Zionism or saying "Free Palestine" gets conflated with hatred of Jewish people, it doesn't protect Jewish people. It protects Israel from accountability."But he emphasised that even though he only did two shows on the tour, if his words succeeded in "turning the conversation back to Palestine, then it was the most successful tour I've ever been on."The controversy also saw US singer Pink, who is Jewish, drawn into the furore after she reposted a message criticising Macklemore.She, too, received massive backlash for her stance, with critics taking aim at everything from her parenting style to past comments about women like Paris Hilton, Britney Spears and Christina Aguilera.She later posted a long statement saying she does not speak for Israel or for any government, and explained her criticism of Macklemore's comments and conduct on stage."Last weekend [Macklemore] stood in front of a stadium full of music-loving families, with violent images from a war on the screens, dedicated a song to the movement of his choice, and then took the mic to tell all of the Jews in the stadium that it wasn't about them.""You don't get to decide that for us," she wrote. Pink also pointed out that in 2014, Macklemore performed his same-sex anthem Same Love at the Grammys, while a mass wedding ceremony saw 33 LGBTQ+ couples get married on stage.But later that year he apologised for a costume he wore which included a black wig, beard and a fake hooked nose, which critics said was antisemitic.

schema.headline: Macklemore dropped from Ed Sheeran tour after 'free Palestine' speech

title: Kevin Pietersen: Why England mentor will bring unfiltered challenge Brendon McCullum needs - Finn
description: I was as surprised as most that Kevin Pietersen has joined the England coaching ranks as a mentor in the build-up to the 50-over World Cup in South Af
body: I was as surprised as most that Kevin Pietersen has joined the England coaching ranks as a mentor in the build-up to the 50-over World Cup in South Africa next autumn. Not only was his last interaction with the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) sitting in the offices at Lord's being told he wouldn't play for England again in 2014, but the success of his YouTube channel, The Switch, and the time it takes to commit to something like that made it seem inconceivable that it could work.However, when I took a step back to remember what it was like to share a dressing room with him at the beginning of my England career, I remembered a number of occasions that lead me to believe this can only be a good thing for all parties. Kevin can be blunt and forthright, but dressing rooms need that in order to function properly. They can't be an echo chamber.On the white-ball tour of India last year, while working for the host broadcaster, he was bemoaning the lack of practice, external that England's players had opted for in the build-up to games. His practice was always intense and with purpose. Usually, he would come up to me as he was walking into the net and say he was going to smash me everywhere and not get out. That would usually rile me up to try to bowl quicker in order to not let him have it his way. He wanted to make sure the practice had that bit more on it, something that is important when steeling your mind and reactions to go out and play at the highest level. I used to enjoy the battles in the nets and it made me a better bowler by having competitive nets against one of the best players in the world. We'd constantly be arguing about what angle the fielders were when he was deciding how many runs he'd scored off that ball, or whether I thought it could have gone to hand when he hit it in the air.Kev was ahead of his time with both his mindset and skills. The inventor of the switch hit, and the most ardent supporter of the IPL before it became mainstream. The flamingo flicks through mid-wicket in Test matches and hitting Glenn McGrath back over his head for six at Lord's in 2005. None of which would look out of place now in 2026. But, he never thought he'd cracked the game. In 2012 when we were in Sri Lanka, I remember turning up for training at the SSC in Colombo to play a warm-up game and Kev had already been there for an hour facing local left-arm spin bowlers in order to try to correct his technique (ironically overseen by Andy Flower) that had been a problem for him intermittently. As a result of that hard work he scored the most remarkable 151 against Rangana Herath in the second Test, hitting him to all parts, and backed it up later that year against India away to seal a historic red-ball series victory where his runs, particularly in Mumbai, formed the bedrock of the win. Those runs and the manner with which they were scored, wouldn't have been possible without those long practice sessions while people weren't watching.It wasn't just about him improving too. In Perth during the 2013-14 Ashes, when Mitchell Johnson and his moustache were running amok, it wouldn't be out of place to see a tailender looking shellshocked at the prospect of having to go and face him in the corner of the dressing room. I vividly remember KP coming over to me (even though I wasn't in the starting XI), and saying 'let's go practice facing the short ball in the nets'. He threw bouncers at my head and helped me figure out a technique to be able to play (mainly evade) the short-pitched bowling. I don't know whether at that stage of the tour he just wanted to be out of the dressing room rather than in it, but it helped me. I can see him doing similar things with players he sees areas of improvement with in his role as mentor.Kevin was never shy of letting the dressing room know his thoughts when debriefing a match, or when discussing the team's approach. I saw this first hand with his dissent towards a fitness fielding session in the build-up to the 2014 Sydney Test match, among others. Some may argue that bringing this into an environment that is clearly working and improving may be a bad thing. However, I believe McCullum has learned from the way the Test team turned a corner as soon as everything seemed in order. Pietersen comes from an era where there was no substitute for hard work and your main way of making a decent living from the game was by playing Test cricket - where you needed to work hard on a fundamental technique in order to firstly survive, but then to build and expand upon to be good at other formats. The balance has clearly shifted now and the power lies with the players able to globetrot and play franchise tournaments. In my eyes the 50-over format is now closer to the pace of modern Test cricket than T20 cricket, helping players with the fundamentals, married up with a strong work ethic can only be a good thing when looking to excel in the format, especially in conditions where there will be passages where the bowlers may be on top.But, I believe he will bring this attitude to the dressing room for the next 14 months leading up to that World Cup.There is no better time to introduce a voice of challenge than now, as it means that the team will not be able to simply maraud on as they have been without checks and balances. Pietersen will provide this, unfiltered.

schema.headline: Kevin Pietersen: Why England mentor will bring unfiltered challenge Brendon McCullum needs - Finn

title: Leeds 4-1 Newcastle: Is 'unplayable' Calvert-Lewin in line for England recall?
description: Newcastle United must be sick of the sight of Dominic Calvert-Lewin.The Leeds United striker has now scored eight times against the club he was previo
body: Newcastle United must be sick of the sight of Dominic Calvert-Lewin.The Leeds United striker has now scored eight times against the club he was previously linked with in years gone by.So you suspect the beleaguered visitors will have been a little relieved to see him substituted late on after he had a hand in two of Leeds' goals in this impressive 4-1 win.Elland Road was unsurprisingly on its feet to hand Calvert-Lewin a deserved standing ovation when he came off.On a night Leeds fans repeatedly taunted Newcastle for spending "all that money" with little return on Monday night, at least, it was a free transfer who caused the visitors real problems with a goal and an assist.So is the 29-year-old making a case for an England recall? Leeds manager Daniel Farke certainly thinks so as he threw his weight behind Calvert-Lewin and a number of others in his side with "English passports"."He's a handful and tough for each and every defender," he said. "He's difficult to play against. He's at a top fitness level. You can see he plays with confidence and a good rhythm, but also benefits from a really strong team and players who work for him."Dominic is a crucial player and if he shows this type of form, he's definitely one of the best strikers in this league. It's the best league in the world and that more or less sums up what I think about him as a player."Calvert-Lewin has been in England head coach Thomas Tuchel's thoughts in recent months.The striker was previously called up by his country back in March after catching the eye in his debut season at Leeds.However, after featuring for England against Uruguay during that particular international window, the striker ultimately missed out on the World Cup in the summer.Ivan Toney and Ollie Watkins instead travelled as captain Harry Kane's deputies.At a time when the marginally older pair are both playing in Saudi Arabia, Calvert-Lewin is staking his claim with his performances closer to home in this country.He has scored three goals in his past four games as the Premier League's leading English striker - just as Tuchel prepares to name his squad on Friday for the upcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain and the Czech Republic.He is also just the second Leeds player to score in five consecutive Premier League appearances at Elland Road after Mark Viduka between March and August 2003.Such was Calvert-Lewin's hunger, he looked dumbfounded after learning his header for Leeds' second against Newcastle had been awarded to team-mate Jayden Bogle after it took a final touch off his team-mate.Former England defender Jamie Carragher was among those watching on impressed following his "almost perfect" display."Maybe sometimes composure has let him down in his career, but not here," he told Sky Sports about the former Everton striker. "He was unplayable."It was right for him and Everton to make a fresh start. As an Evertonian you are probably thinking why didn't we keep him."Sometimes a move rejuvenates a player. He is the type of player you think as an ex-centre-back, I am glad I am not playing now."No side will relish coming up against Calvert-Lewin and this aggressive Leeds outfit at Elland Road this season. In fact, only Arsenal (52), Manchester City (50), Manchester United (45) and Bournemouth (37) have won more Premier League points in 2026 than Leeds United (35), with the Whites suffering just a single defeat across their past 13 league matches.Yet Newcastle's implosion was remarkable as a young team were bullied and outfought.Newcastle had previously made a good start under head coach Matthias Jaissle, following so much change in the summer, and were unbeaten in their opening five games in all competitions before this reality check.But they have faced more shots than any other side in the Premier League.However clinical Newcastle were in the opening weeks of the campaign, they mustered just eight efforts on target against Liverpool, Tottenham Hotspur and Bournemouth before their trip to Elland Road.That was a dangerous cocktail going into this game.What was most galling, though, was the visitors' failure to match Leeds' bite at a raucous Elland Road. Jaissle's side crumbled and conceded three goals in a chastening 14-minute period in the first half.It was a night the German manager swore in his post-match news conference to illustrate how low he felt."I don't want to point fingers and point any players out tonight," he said. "We were not matching as a team the level of intensity, the level of duel behaviours, the level of physicality."This is something we need to bring on the pitch in every match. This is non-negotiable. It should be the basic fundamentals of football."These are young lads. The learning curve needs to be fast."For Calvert-Lewin and Leeds, however, this was a night to remember.

schema.headline: Leeds 4-1 Newcastle: Is 'unplayable' Calvert-Lewin in line for England recall?

title: F1 Q&A: Madring's overtaking problem, virtual safety car operation and will there be any rookies in 2027?
description: Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli stretched his lead in the drivers' standings with victory at the first Spanish Grand Prix held at the Madring.Max Verstappen
body: Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli stretched his lead in the drivers' standings with victory at the first Spanish Grand Prix held at the Madring.Max Verstappen finished second in the Red Bull and McLaren's Lando Norris completed the top three.Norris, who was leading, lost out having passed the pit entry immediately before the virtual safety car was called.BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.The new Madring circuit looks like one of the worst on the calendar for entertaining racing. Given that half the track is custom built (ie not having to conform to street layouts), how did they get it so wrong and will substantial changes be made ahead of next year? - MattIt's a good question. Even before the race weekend began, drivers were predicting that overtaking would be next to impossible at the new Madring, and they were proved right.The track is effectively a start-from-scratch layout built partly as a new track and partly on existing roads around the Ifema exhibition centre near Madrid's Barajas international airport.It is, therefore, mystifying as to how they got it so wrong, as the problems could be  foreseen by anyone with an understanding of F1. As Lando Norris put it witheringly after the race: "I don't know how someone looks at this design and goes: 'Mint.'"There are some key issues.The main one is the lack of a long straight leading into a big braking zone.Another is, as the drivers pointed out, a lot of the corners have entries where drivers have to combine braking and turning, which makes overtaking extremely difficult, as well as walls that come back towards the track on corner exit.And another is the ultra-long pit lane - the longest on the calendar.The longer a pit lane, the more the time loss for a pit stop, so the less chance of having more than a one-stop race. And if tyre degradation is high, that means more tyre management, driving further under the limit, and less chance of accidents and therefore safety cars.The good news is it is not hard to see how it could be fixed.As Norris said: "There's a lot of opportunity. They can make it into a track that's good for racing, and I'm excited to come back here next year if they can make these changes because I think it's a track that is good fun to drive and it can be a great race track."To me, it's not a great race track. It's great in qualifying."Norris suggested removing turns 18 and 19 and "making a straight line from 17 to 20, have a much wider entry like Austin Turn One or Turn 10 in Austin... big hairpin".That, he said, would "create much better opportunities for everyone and you'll be able to enjoy the race".He also advocated what he called "some trickier changes", such as changing the unpopular, clumsy chicane at Turn Five, and the section from there to Turn Seven.While they're at it, it would also be worth looking at the location and layout of the pits and paddock.This was more fractured and over a much larger area than at any other track, which made working for F1 personnel difficult in a number of ways.The many large exhibition halls on what is, frankly, a pretty unprepossessing site - it's a bit like holding a grand prix at the NEC in Birmingham - clearly don't make this the easiest task.But finding a location for a pit lane that is not split in half by a building and making it somewhere the pits and paddock can be together and entirely outside would be another step in the right direction.The virtual safety car (VSC) definitely throws jeopardy into races, but it does not do virtually what the safety car does. Would it not be more balanced to have a minimum of at least one full lap? Yes, this would dampen the jeopardy effect but what happened to Lando Norris feels like a chance card in Monopoly. - KyleLando Norris' bad luck with the virtual safety car at the Spanish Grand Prix has certainly focused attention on the ways this can disrupt races.The VSC has always had issues - it freezes a race rather than resets it, which can be a bit boring compared to an actual safety car - but it has the benefit of minimising disruption when a track hazard can be cleared relatively quickly.It has long been an opportunity for someone to benefit over a rival, because making a pit stop under a VSC takes significantly less time than under racing conditions.But usually this has been in cases where one team has changed or deployed its strategy with the express intention of waiting for a safety car or VSC (such as Norris himself in his maiden victory in Miami in 2024), and benefiting over a rival who has run a more conventional strategy.That sort of thing is considered fair game. What happened to Norris - a driver lost a race win because his specific track positioning at the time of a VSC meant he alone was unable to pit under it - is, to the best anyone could remember on Sunday, unique.The media are not privy to conversations in drivers' briefings, and Norris in particular gets a bit sniffy when information from those meetings leaks out because they are meant to be a safe space where the drivers and FIA can share opinions without it becoming a controversy.But it emerged after the race that this issue, as Norris put it, "has been spoken about many, many times".Whether Norris' misfortune leads to a change, such as ensuring that a VSC is deployed for at least one whole lap, remains to be seen.There is no easy answer, because within F1 it's recognised that safety cars are part of the competitive jigsaw, and can be used to a team's advantage. And the latest rules have been arrived at after various previous iterations that worked in different ways, such as shutting the pit lane for specific periods.McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said:  "Offering a personal opinion, I'm puzzled myself as to what's right. "Is it correct to give enough duration such that everyone will have been subject to the same track conditions? So, for instance, the virtual safety car lasts at least one full lap. "Or you just keep it in the hands of the Gods, and sometimes you are lucky, sometimes you are not. I'm not sure."There is process for these sorts of discussions - they go to a sporting advisory committee for analysis, before being reviewed by the F1 Commission of teams, commercial rights holder F1 and governing body the FIA.That won't happen quickly - unless it is decided by F1 and the FIA that it is a desirable outcome to change the rules. Right now, the momentum for that does not appear to be there.What are the prospects for rookies coming into Formula 1 next year? Many drivers are re-signing long contracts with their teams. Are there likely to be any new recruits? - MiaThe most likely place for a new driver to come into F1 next season is Haas, where Esteban Ocon's position looks shaky.The two main candidates there are Italy's reigning Formula 2 champion Leonardo Fornaroli, who is part of McLaren's driver development programme, and Brazilian Rafael Camara, who is second in F2 this year and part of the Ferrari driver academy.Both have tested for Haas and are said to have impressed the team.Haas will want a quick driver who brings money, and it's not clear who the favourite is. Ryo Hirakawa, Haas' reserve driver and a long-time protege of Haas' technical partner Toyota, is also in the picture, but considered a less likely candidate.Elsewhere, there is talk of Red Bull considering moving F2 championship leader Nikola Tsolov, who is Bulgarian, into their Racing Bulls team.To do so, they would have to drop either Liam Lawson or Arvid Lindblad. It's hard to see how it would be Lindblad, after such an impressive rookie campaign.But Lawson has also been doing a good job this year, so it's not a given.At Cadillac, they have Indycar race-winner Colton Herta as reserve. They have been planning for Herta to be in F1 before too long - the idea behind him moving to Europe and doing Formula 2 this year was so he could learn the ropes on this side of the Atlantic and be as prepared as possible for graduation to F1.But Herta has had a very difficult F2 campaign this year - his best result is a fifth place and he is 19th in the championship - so moving him up to F1 for 2027 would be a massive risk.Ugo Ugochukwu, who won the Formula 3 title in Madrid on Sunday, is another American said to be of interest to Cadillac.He had been part of the McLaren driver development programme for several years until they parted ways at the end of last season.But even if Ugochukwu's Cadillac links become formalised, next year is probably too early for him to make F1.He's also extremely tall - well over six foot and much taller even than Ocon, Alex Albon and George Russell, the current tallest drivers - so getting him into an F1 car would not be easy.The other teams are pretty much locked down, although it's still unknown whether Fernando Alonso is going to continue in F1 next year.

schema.headline: F1 Q&A: Madring's overtaking problem, virtual safety car operation and will there be any rookies in 2027?

title: Newspaper headlines: Reform donors 'could face enhanced checks' and 'Sydney Sweeney blasted'
description: The Guardian, external and the Times, external lead on the government's plans to introduce stricter residency checks for people donating to political
body: The Guardian, external and the Times, external lead on the government's plans to introduce stricter residency checks for people donating to political parties – a move that could block the £72m given to Reform UK by two cryptocurrency tycoons. A source tells the Times that potential donors might have to prove that they've lived in the UK for at least 183 days a year. In a separate article the paper says Reform is already spending the money, it's doubling its policy team from 10 to 20, recruiting 400 field agents and preparing its YouTube channel.In an editorial the Daily Mail, external accuses Labour of "hyperventilating hypocrisy". The paper says there's nothing to prove that the two tycoons are seeking to benefit from their gifts to Reform, whereas Labour depends on funding from trade unions and it rewards them with changes to legislation that favour their members.The Daily Mirror, external says the Reform leader, Nigel Farage can rail against the rules and attack the establishment as much as he likes. The paper says "the floundering leader propped up by two billionaires" cannot expect voters to stop asking whose interests his party would really serve in power.The village of Piddington in Oxfordshire, where people are protesting against a plan to build a camp for asylum seekers, is on the front pages of the Daily Express, external and Daily Telegraph, external. The Express says the campaign group Women of Piddington has written about security fears to all 266 female MPs, but only four have responded.The i Paper, external says a review commissioned by the government will say that ADHD is not being widely overdiagnosed. However, the report – to be published within weeks – will say that record numbers of people are seeking an official diagnosis in order to access support and benefits.According to the Financial Times, external, France has stunned other EU countries with a request to remove the Russian-Uzbek oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the list of people and organisations targeted by European sanctions. The paper says France's move is linked to its efforts to secure the release of a number of French citizens imprisoned in Azerbaijan.And finally, the Telegraph, external reports that Halloween pumpkins will be too small to carve this year, after drought damaged their growth. Farmers say they'll be about 40% smaller than usual.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: Reform donors 'could face enhanced checks' and 'Sydney Sweeney blasted'

title: Emmys 2026: Memorable moments and what you didn't see on TV
description: Memorable moments from the Emmys and everything you couldn't see on TVFigure caption, Watch: Highlights from the 2026 Emmy Awards, a star-studded and
body: Memorable moments from the Emmys and everything you couldn't see on TVFigure caption, Watch: Highlights from the 2026 Emmy Awards, a star-studded and record-breaking nightByNardine SaadReporting fromat the Emmy Awards in Los AngelesUpdated 3 hours agoWelsh actor Matthew Rhys and US actress Jean Smart made Emmy Awards history during TV's biggest night in Hollywood this year, which brought out stars from the small screen, film, sport and music. Hosted by Law & Order SVU star Mariska Hargitay - the first woman to host in 15 years - the ceremony was packed with cameos from celebrities, emotional speeches, touching tributes and plenty of banter.Backstage, the winners continued their celebrations offscreen and answered questions about their wins and some of the ceremony's most viral moments. Here's a look at some of the viral moments and all the bits and pieces the BBC captured behind-the-scenes at the show:Widow's Bay reflects on being a sleeper hit and owning the night Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The cast of Widow's Bay chatted backstage about being the standout winner at this year's Emmy Awards The cast and crew behind Apple TV's sleeper hit celebrated the supernatural TV comedy's popular first season, which nabbed six wins on Monday and another eight at the Creative Arts Emmys earlier this month. Asked about the show being relatively smaller and unknown to some audiences, the cast and creators reflected backstage with gratitude for the grassroots efforts to promote the show through word-of-mouth early on. "All the people online talking about it, or viewers, or people just tweeting about it, truly like it. That really got the word to spread, and we're so grateful," said writer and creator Katie Dippold.Rhys quipped that those people were "predominantly our parents"."I honestly think we're just happy that everyone reacted to the scripts the way we did when we read them, and that's all to thanks to this team," Rhys said.He said the series was on a "giddy ascent" ahead of the Emmys. Dippold joked that she was terrified thinking that the show might get even more attention with all their Emmy wins. What it's like 'backstage'Image caption, The awards sit on a table across the street from the show, where winners will come to get them engraved The BBC had a team at the Peacock Theatre in downtown Los Angeles, which was shutdown to traffic and onlookers as celebrities in black cars took over.Droves of celebrity handlers dressed in black - from their security details to publicists - were posted throughout the area - which also sits across from Crypto.com Arena (home to the LA Lakers). While the ceremony and red carpet is mostly confined to the Peacock Theater, the set-up around it is vast.Next door at the JW Marriott hotel, ballrooms are converted into press workspaces where celebrities and their teams milled about throughout the ceremony, reuniting cast-mates who haven't seen each other since they wrapped filming.The road to this area is long, windy and done on foot. Once a winner accepts their prize on TV, they are taken across the street to get their awards engraved, take photos and chat with reporters. They are escorted through a series of covered spaces, where they pop into one ballroom specifically for photos, another to speak with print and digital media and then another section cordoned off just for TV interviews. This area also is home to where winners get their awards engraved. Dozens of golden Emmy statues were set up on tables here, which passerbys (including yours truly) can readily gawk at and take photos of. So, in every way, "backstage" isn't really "backstage" at the Emmys. It's more like "next door". An Emmy statue on the red (blue?) carpet Image source, Getty ImagesIn a sea of glamorous gowns and tuxedoes, Hacks star Megan Stalter, who was nominated for best comedy supporting actress, arrived on the Emmys blue carpet gilded as an Emmy statuette.The actress, who has repeatedly turned heads with her red-carpet looks, donned gold body paint and angel wings for the look and held up an enormous version of the atom hoisted by the statuette during arrivals.Stalter dodged questions about what inspired the look, telling reporters that she and her stylist just threw it together and that her co-star Paul W Downs airbrushed her himself.Figure caption, Watch: Selena Gomez, Zendaya and other stars light up Emmys red carpetKate O'Flynn wants to see your Widow's Bay Halloween costumesImage source, Getty ImagesWidow's Bay star Kate O'Flynn told reporters backstage that she was "completely gobsmacked" and "on top of the world" by her win in the spooky comedy, which centres on the strange happenings of a haunted New England island.She said that her character - Patricia, the assistant to Mayor Tom Loftis (played by Matthew Rhys) - has an "awkwardness", "bravery and humour" that resonated with audiences."I think everyone just has felt like Patricia in that way," she says.She says she was pleasantly surprised by "an army" of people who turned up dressed as her character at this year's DragonCon."So I'm excited to see Halloween and all the antlers come out and take over the world," she joked to reporters backstage. Speaking to the BBC, the British actress had a message for everyone back home: "Just to our family and friends, we did it. It's great. I don't know what to say. I don't know."'100% sure I wasn't going to win' - Allison Janney's face became a meme Image source, Getty ImagesWhen Allison Janney's name was announced as the winner for best supporting actress in drama, the camera panned to The Diplomat star with her mouth open and both hands cupping the sides of her face. She remained for several second before getting up, still surprised, and covering her mouth in shock. "Oh my God," the fictional president was seen mouthing as she made her way to the stage. With The Pitt flooding the supporting actress in a drama series category, the medical drama seemed poised to have one of its stars take home the prize. Janney, who plays the US President Grace Penn in political drama The Diplomat, told reporters backstage that she was "genuinely shocked" by her win because of how big of a show The Pitt had become."We really didn't think it was going to go my way. So I felt just excited and relaxed," she said, because she was "100% sure I wasn't gonna win".Matthew Rhys jokes about his rivalry with partner Keri RussellImage source, Getty ImagesWelsh actor Matthew Rhys refused to go backstage and talk with reporters until he found out whether Widow's Bay director Hiro Murai won in the directing category (he did). When he finally made his way to the microphone, Rhys specifically called on the BBC for the first question."The BBC, surely!" he said, before reflecting on making history and becoming the first person to win two Emmy awards for best lead actor in the same year - for roles in Widow's Bay and the psychological thriller The Beast In Me."At the moment, I genuinely can't quite believe what's just happened," he said. "I hope to reflect on it tomorrow."He also teased the friendly competition between him and his partner, actress Keri Russell, who was up for an Emmy for her role in The Diplomat this year."It's not great. I bet a lot of money on myself. The kids ran a book," he joked, adding,  "It's going to be a rough week for her. I'm sorry. I don't know if I am."He joked, waving around the trophy, that Russell is his better half and "always the class act"."She's always really the winner, if I'm perfectly honest."Host Mariska Hargitay taps Taylor Swift and NBA star for skitsImage source, Getty ImagesHost Mariska Hargitay tapped a handful of celebrities during her hosting debut, including Taylor Swift, Jalen Brunson and Broadway star Andrew Rannells. The Law & Order SVU star opened the show with a musical number based on Joan Jett and the Blackheart's I Love Rock & Roll, name-checking many of the shows and stars of the night, while singing "I love TV screens".NBA star Jalen Brunson made a cameo, a nod to Hargitay's love of the New York Knicks basketball team. Later, in a pre-recorded skit, Hargitay and her costars from Law & Order SVU tried to solve the mystery of whether Taylor Swift would appear at the Emmys.Swift then appeared, joining in as a character trying to solve the case, which took viewers on a tour of the nominees and Swift's album and personal life.The skit closed with Hargitay, Swift and one of her cats, who is named Olivia Benson, after Hargitay's character on the Law & Order series.DTF St Louis star isn't watching the show, but knows all the mums areImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, DTF St Louis stars Jason Bateman, Richard Jenkins, Arlan Ruf, David Harbour, Linda Cardellini and Joy SundayDTF St Louis star Arlan Ruf, who plays David Harbour's son on the dark comedy miniseries, made some jokes about the primary demographic fans of the HBO series, which centres on a murder stemming from a dating app.  "I don't know a lot of my friends are watching it," he says cheekily, adding that "their mums are". Ruf adds that his friends' mums have been telling him how great it is, a nod to the large female audience for true crime. "So every friend's mom I know is watching," he says.

schema.headline: Emmys 2026: Memorable moments and what you didn't see on TV

title: Bob Mackie: Legendary costume designer dies aged 87
description: Image source, Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bob Mackie at a red carpet event in Los Angeles in JanuaryByTiffany Wertheimer an
body: Image source, Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bob Mackie at a red carpet event in Los Angeles in JanuaryByTiffany Wertheimer and Jack BurgessBob Mackie, who designed dazzling costumes for stars including Cher, Tina Turner, Dolly Parton and Elton John has died, aged 87.The US fashion designer, known as the "Sultan of Sequins" for his sparkling creations, won a Tony Award, nine Emmys and received three Oscar nominations during his career."It is with a heavy heart that we share the news that Mr Bob Mackie passed away today," a statement on his Instagram account announced on Monday."He lived his 87 years to the fullest, fulfilling his dream of being a Fashion and Costume Designer, which is all he ever wanted to do," it added. "His genius and extraordinary designs will live on forever, continuing to bring beauty into this world."Mackie was particularly influential in Cher's career and designed her iconic Mohawk outfit, which she wore to the Oscars in 1986. It became known as her "revenge" outfit, because she wasn't nominated for anything.The showgirl-inspired costume featured a plumed mohawk headdress and showed Cher's bare midriff - a very new, and very shocking look at the time.The costume has gone down in fashion history as one of the most outrageous and  extravagant ever to appear at the awards."I didn't get nominated for a movie that everyone thought I would actually win for [Mask] - so was dressing that night for a kind of revenge," Cher explained in the 2024 documentary Bob Mackie: Naked Illusion.Mackie told the BBC in 2010 that when Cher started out she "looked like no-one else in the entertainment business at the time"."Everybody just went crazy over this woman as she could wear anything," he added.Cher was widely reported to be the first woman to show her belly button on US television - and Mackie's designs were pivotal to that. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Cher's infamous mohawk "revenge" outfit at the 1986 OscarsMackie was also the creative genius behind several of Sir Elton John's costumes, including his now-iconic Dodgers baseball outfit - bedazzled of course - that he wore during his performances at Dodger Stadium in Los Angeles in 1975."Every time I put something on that Bob made, I felt very, very special," Sir John wrote on Instagram. "His costumes were works of art, and he will go down as one of the most legendary designers ever in Hollywood."Singer Pink wore many of his designs over the years. Sharing several of the outfits she wore on stage during her Funhouse tour in 2009, she wrote "I was so lucky to be dressed by him for so long. He was loving, wickedly funny and an absolute genius.""There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels."Mackie was still designing up until recently - Sabrina Carpenter wore one of his designs at the MTV Video Music Awards last year.He also designed the dress Miley Cyrus wore during her performance at the 2024 Grammy Awards. She won a Grammy that year for her break-up anthem, Flowers - perhaps it was her own version of a "revenge" dress.Image source, John Shearer/Getty Images for The Recording AcademyImage caption, Miley Cyrus wore her own style of Mackie "revenge" dress at the 2024 Grammy AwardsRobert Gordon Mackie was born in Monterey Park, California, in 1939.His design career started as a sketch artist for Jean Louis, a French-American costume designer. One of Mackie's early assignments saw him sketch the dress that Marilyn Monroe wore when she delivered her breathy rendition of "Happy Birthday Mr President" to John F Kennedy in 1962.He married Hollywood singer and actress Lulu Porter in 1960, but they divorced three years later. They had a son together, Robin, who died in his early thirties from an Aids related illness.Mackie was in a relationship with Iranian fashion designer, Ray Aghayan, from 1963 until Aghayan's death in 2011."I think I'm the oldest living designer in Hollywood," Mackie told The Guardian in 2018. When asked if he'd ever retire, his answer was simple - "I hope not."Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, "There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels," Pink wrote in a tribute to Bob Mackie. The singer wore many of his designs over the years, especially during her Funhouse Tour in 2009Slide 1 of 7, Pink performs the final UK leg of her Funhouse tour on stage at O2 Arena on December 8, 2009 in London, England. , "There are going to be some fabulously dressed angels," Pink wrote in a tribute to Bob Mackie. The singer wore many of his designs over the years, especially during her Funhouse Tour in 2009

title: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards
description: US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) are a "hoax", as he criticised calls to have more guardrails
body: US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of artificial intelligence (AI) are a "hoax", as he criticised calls to have more guardrails in place for the fast-moving technology.It comes after Jack Clark, co-founder of AI giant Anthropic, told the BBC that a "kill switch" that can be checked by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.Clark's comments followed warnings about the risks the technology poses to humanity that have been raised in recent days by several executives and staff at leading AI firms.Those concerns triggered a selloff in tech firms' shares as investors weighed the impact of a potential slowdown in the multi-billion dollar development of AI.In a series of social media posts, the US president compared warnings about AI to the "Global Warming Scam" which, he said, was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats".Trump also called himself "the Hoax Buster", likening concerns about the safety of the technology to what he called "the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX".The only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president, said Trump.In another post he wrote: "There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China. WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!"Chinese state media said experts had warned that "Washington's growing anxiety over China's rapid AI development appears to be increasingly distorting its policy priorities"."They know that China has become a strong competitor in AI, and worry that if the US slows down development or tightens regulation, China could catch up even faster," Xin Qiang, a professor of American Studies at Fudan University, told the Global Times.Clark, who is one of Anthropic's seven founders, said earlier on Monday that a way of shutting off AI software completely if it gets too dangerous was something society "might want to eventually pass rules around".He added that "most labs have different ways of being able to pull the plug", including Anthropic, but said lawmakers may need to enforce having one.UK Business Secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on Tuesday that people should "never be complacent" about the impact AI might have but added: "We've got to be careful not to get hyperbolic about this either."Speaking to the BBC, he said: "Of course there are risks but, let's be frank, there are some tremendous upsides, whether it's public services, healthcare, the contribution to the economy."

schema.headline: Trump says AI safety fears a 'hoax' as he rejects calls for greater safeguards

title: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
description: When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning"."I was absolutely li
body: When Brianna Beyrouti looks back on her former life in the city of Portland, Oregon, she says she had been financially "drowning"."I was absolutely living paycheque to paycheque. Every time the smallest thing came up, it was like 'Oh, gosh, the kids need shoes, how am I going to afford that?' As a single parent, everything falls on my shoulders."Last year, Brianna left Portland and its metropolitan population of 2.5 million people. She and her two children moved 2,000 miles east to Muncie, Indiana, a small city with 65,000 people, a university and lots of open space, taking advantage of a scheme that contributed $5,000 towards the cost of the move to boost population growth.The relocation has been a revelation for her finances. She continues to work remotely for the same bank, so her annual salary of $107,000 (£79,000) is unchanged, but she has been able to buy a home for the first time. And her mortgage is less than she used to have to pay in rent.In Portland she was paying rent of $1,290 a month for an apartment, while the combined cost of her mortgage, home insurance and property tax for her detached home in Muncie is $1,100.Add the fact that state income tax is lower in Indiana, and that her car insurance and energy bills have also fallen, and Brianna says she is $600 a month better off."I'm able to live my life more than I was before," she says. "When my kids want something, I'm much more inclined to say yes. My quality of life has increased dramatically."To help it stand out from the crowd, and encourage remote workers to move there from outside Indiana, Muncie's local council offers them $5,000 in cash to cover their relocation costs.It does this via a website called MakeMyMove, which lists several such relocation support schemes offered by similar small cities and towns across the US. These pay MakeMyMove a subscription fee.Other incentives locations offer potential new residents are complementary cinema tickets, restaurant vouchers, and even free bottles of wine.Brianna and her children are one of around 100 families to have moved to Muncie through the MakeMyMove programme. She says she hadn't heard of the city before.Across the US, MakeMyMove says it helped 1,000 people in total relocate last year, and is on target to increase that to 1,500 in 2026.Scientist Elena Chrysostomou also used a relocation support scheme to swap a big city for a small town. In 2024 she relocated from San Diego, California, to Jacksonville, a town of 17,700 people in rural Illinois.The move was backed by the Jacksonville Regional Economic Development Corporation (JREDC), which gave her $5,000 in cash, plus a "quality of life package" worth $4,000 that includes free gym memberships and golf passes.The JREDC says that while the region is "already a great place to live", the support scheme helps to "sweeten the deal".Elena was spending $3,000 renting a one-bedroom apartment in San Diego, but she now owns a three-bedroom home, with a mortgage of $1,868. At the same time, her salary has gone up 22% after she changed jobs, and her commute has gone down from a 15-minute drive to one of just one minute."I never thought that I'd be able to afford a house on my own, I always thought I'd need a partner, and even then, in San Diego, it would be so tough," she says."It's just more freeing. There's more security and independence."While both she and Brianna have no regrets, they do admit to some drawbacks to their new lives. These include the narrower range of activities and restaurant choices, leaving behind friends and family, and for Brianna the difficulty of settling her children into new schools.And while in Portland Brianna enjoyed walking to parks and shops, she now relies on her car to get anywhere.But overall she says she is thrilled. "I have the biggest savings I've ever had in my life, and I'm a homeowner, and I can do things with my kids – we actually went on vacation for the first time in my youngest's life."Have you moved for a better life? Get in touch.

schema.headline: I got paid $5,000 to move to a place I'd never heard of
